key_insight: Use simulation to filter which segments of human videos are physically executable by a target robot, then learn modular policies (grasp + post-grasp) from the filtered data so robots can imitate realistic human motions even with non-human hands.
problem_solved: Human videos provide rich signals for post-grasp manipulation but often contain grasps that robots cannot physically perform; this work solves how to reliably leverage human video data for robot prehensile manipulation by selecting only simulation-feasible demonstrations and training modular controllers.
method: Automatically parse human videos into grasp and post-grasp segments and propose candidate robot grasps.
Simulate candidate grasps and filter out video segments that are not physically executable by the target robot (simulation-filtering).
Train modular policies: a grasping policy (from simulation/robot data) and a post-grasp imitation policy (from filtered human video segments), then combine them for execution.
impact: Enables large-scale use of widely available human video data for robot manipulation while avoiding infeasible demonstrations, lowering the need for costly robot-specific data and speeding development of practical manipulation policies.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: human video -> segmentation (grasp/post-grasp) -> simulation filter -> modular policy -> robot execution
Before/after comparison: success rates or qualitative outcomes with vs. without simulation filtering
Illustration comparing human hand pose to robot gripper mapping and filtered vs. rejected video frames
Sequence visualization of a single task: human clip, filtered grasp, learned robot execution
paper_title: Imitating What Works: Simulation-Filtered Modular Policy Learning from Human Videos
paper_authors: Albert J. Zhai, Kuo-Hao Zeng, Jiasen Lu, Ali Farhadi, Shenlong Wang
